341.title: The three classification tests specified in the Grade 4 competency

members.title: The three classification tests specified in the Grade 4 competency
members.content: The figure shows three separate experiments designed to classify materials. The first experiment displays two materials: absorbent cloth, paper, and sponge on the left, and non-absorbent plastic, glass, and metal on the right. The second experiment shows a wooden and plastic float alongside a stone and metal sink, with the materials placed in water to observe whether they float or sink. Finally, the third experiment presents two groups of materials: decaying leaves, food scraps, paper, and wood on one side, and materials that do not decay – plastic, glass, metal, and rubber – on the other.

members.title: Properties of Materials (Part 1 of 3)
members.content:
Every material can be described by the way it looks, feels, and behaves.
These descriptions are its properties.
When learners in the elementary grades sort materials, they are not memorizing lists — they are using a property as a rule for putting things into groups.

members.title: Properties of Materials (Part 2 of 3)
members.content:
This skill is introduced in Grade 3 with the physical properties of solid materials, and is extended in Grade 4 into three specific classification tests that learners can actually perform in the classroom.
Physical properties can be observed without changing what the material is made of.

members.title: Properties of Materials (Part 3 of 3)
members.content:
The Grade 3 competency names three that learners can check by hand: whether a material is hard (a stone, a coin), shiny (a new spoon, aluminum foil, a tansan), or stretchable (a rubber band, a garter, a balloon).
Other familiar physical properties are color, texture, size, weight, and flexibility.
Chemical properties describe how a material behaves when it reacts or changes into something new.

members.title: The Grade 4 competency names three
members.content: The Grade 4 competency names three: whether a material can be burned, whether it reacts with other materials, and whether it is degradable or biodegradable. These properties cannot be seen at a glance; they show themselves only when the material is exposed to fire, air, moisture, or other substances.

341.title: Ability to absorb water. Place a drop of water on the material and watch what happens. If the

members.title: Ability to absorb water. Place a drop of water on the material and watch what happens. If the
members.content: water soaks in and the material becomes damp, the material is absorbent. If the water stays on the surface as a bead and can be wiped off, the material is non-absorbent. Cloth, paper, sponge, cotton, and wood absorb water; plastic, glass, metal, and rubber do not.

341.title: Ability to float or sink. Place the material gently in a basin of water. Materials that stay on the

members.title: Ability to float or sink. Place the material gently in a basin of water. Materials that stay on the
members.content: surface float; materials that go down to the bottom sink. Dry wood, plastic bottle caps, styrofoam, and dry leaves float. Stone, coins, nails, and marbles sink. Learners often expect size to decide this, so it is worth showing them a large piece of wood that floats and a small nail that sinks.

341.title: Ability to undergo decay. Materials that rot, break down, and return to the soil over time are said

members.title: Ability to undergo decay. Materials that rot, break down, and return to the soil over time are said
members.content: to undergo decay, or to be biodegradable. Food scraps, leaves, paper, and wood decay. Plastic, glass, metal, and rubber do not decay within a useful length of time, so they are called non- biodegradable. This test cannot be finished in one class period; it is usually set up as a week-long or month-long observation using two buried samples.

341.title: Grouping the Same Materials in Different Ways

members.title: Grouping the Same Materials in Different Ways
members.content:
There is no single correct way to group a set of materials. The grouping depends on which property is being used as the rule.
Consider six items commonly available in a Filipino classroom:
Reading the table down each column gives a different pair of groups each time. The basahan joins the dried leaf and the wood under one rule, but joins the plastic bag under another. This is the central idea of the lesson: a material has several properties at once, and the group it belongs to changes with the question being asked.

members.title: being used as the rule. Consider six items commonly available in a Filipino classroom:
members.section_title: Grouping the Same Materials in Different Ways
members.content: The table shows six different materials arranged in three columns. The first column lists the materials: basahan, plastic sando bag, dried leaf, tansan, piece of wood, and marble. The second and third columns describe their properties in relation to water and decay. The basahan floats at first, then sinks, and if made of cotton, it undergoes decay. The plastic sando bag floats and does not undergo decay. The dried leaf floats and does undergo decay, and the tansan, which is a bottle cap, sinks and does not undergo decay.

members.title: Why Grouping Matters (Part 1 of 3)
members.content:
Use, Handling, and Disposal
People choose materials for a purpose because of their properties.
A raincoat and a payong are made of plastic or coated cloth because those materials do not absorb water.
A bimpo and a basahan are made of cotton because cotton does.

members.title: Why Grouping Matters (Part 2 of 3)
members.content:
A banca is made of wood because wood floats.
Knowing the property explains the choice.
Grouping also decides how waste should be handled, which is the point of the Grade 3 competency on proper disposal.
Biodegradable waste such as vegetable peelings and fallen leaves can be composted and returned to the garden as fertilizer.

members.title: Why Grouping Matters (Part 3 of 3)
members.content:
Non-biodegradable waste such as plastic bottles, tin cans, and glass must be cleaned and set aside for recycling, because it will not break down on its own.
This is the science behind the familiar nabubulok and di-nabubulok labels on segregation bins in schools and barangays.

347.title: Changes in solid materials when bent, pressed, hammered, and cut

members.title: Changes in solid materials when bent, pressed, hammered, and cut
members.content: The image shows four distinct ways a solid material can be altered. The first shows a shape change where a long piece is bent into a curve, but the overall size remains the same. Next, a flat piece is shown being pressed, resulting in a flattened shape and the original amount of material remaining unchanged. The third depicts a piece of metal being hammered, which causes it to become flattened and widened, and importantly, the metal itself remains solid. Finally, the image displays a piece being cut, resulting in two smaller pieces, each retaining the same material as the original.

347.title: Bending changes the shape of a material while its size stays the same. A wire, a plastic straw, a

members.title: Bending changes the shape of a material while its size stays the same. A wire, a plastic straw, a
members.content:
paper clip, and a strip of cardboard can all be bent. Materials that bend without breaking are flexible;
materials such as chalk, glass, and dry twigs are rigid and snap instead.

347.title: Pressing squeezes a material and flattens it. Dough pressed by the palm spreads out and becomes

members.title: Pressing squeezes a material and flattens it. Dough pressed by the palm spreads out and becomes
members.content: wider and thinner, though the amount of dough has not changed. A tin can stepped on during a game of tumbang preso becomes crumpled: its shape changes while the metal remains metal.

347.title: Hammering delivers a stronger, sharper force. A piece of soft metal that is hammered becomes

members.title: Hammering delivers a stronger, sharper force. A piece of soft metal that is hammered becomes
members.content: flatter and wider, which is how a panday shapes a bolo or a tansan is flattened into a washer. Brittle materials such as stone and glass do not flatten when hammered; they break into pieces.

347.title: Cutting divides a material into smaller parts, so the change is mainly in size. Paper cut with scissors

members.title: Cutting divides a material into smaller parts, so the change is mainly in size. Paper cut with scissors
members.content: becomes several smaller papers. Cloth cut by a mananahi becomes the pieces of a garment. Each piece is still made of exactly the same material as before.

347.title: Changes Caused by Heat and by Oxygen (Part 1 of 3)

members.title: Changes Caused by Heat and by Oxygen (Part 1 of 3)
members.content:
The Grade 5 competency moves from force to two conditions that cause deeper changes: application of heat and the presence or lack of oxygen.
Heat can cause a material to melt, evaporate, soften, harden, or burn.
Ice left on a saucer melts into water.

members.title: Changes Caused by Heat and by Oxygen (Part 2 of 3)
members.content:
Candle wax melts and then hardens again when it cools.
Sugar heated in a pan turns brown and gives off a sweet smell as it becomes caramel — and that change cannot be undone.
Oxygen is part of the air around us, and many changes depend on whether it is present.

members.title: Changes Caused by Heat and by Oxygen (Part 3 of 3)
members.content:
Iron exposed to air and moisture forms a reddish-brown coating called rust, which is why a bakal na pako left outdoors during the rainy season looks nothing like a new one.
A candle covered by a glass jar goes out because the oxygen inside is used up.
Sliced saging or mansanas turns brown when left on the table because its exposed flesh reacts with the oxygen in the air.

members.title: Reversible and Irreversible Changes (Part 1 of 3)
members.content:
By Grade 6, learners sort changes into two kinds.
A physical change alters only the appearance of a material — its size, shape, or state — while the material itself stays the same.

members.title: Reversible and Irreversible Changes (Part 2 of 3)
members.content:
Physical changes are usually reversible: melted ice can be frozen again, a crumpled paper can be flattened, and dissolved salt can be recovered by evaporating the water.
A chemical change produces an entirely new material with new properties.

members.title: Reversible and Irreversible Changes (Part 3 of 3)
members.content:
Chemical changes are irreversible: rust cannot be turned back into shiny iron, burnt wood cannot be turned back into wood, and a cooked egg cannot be uncooked.
Useful clues that a chemical change has taken place are a new color, a new smell, bubbles of gas, heat given off, or a solid forming where there was none.

members.title: A chemical change produces an entirely new material with new properties. Chemical changes are

The second row details the cause for each change: force for bending a wire and cutting paper, heat for melting ice, and heat and oxygen for burning wood into uling. members.title: Useful and Harmful Changes (Part 1 of 3)
members.content:
The last Grade 4 competency asks learners to judge a change, not just describe it.
Many changes are useful.
Cutting cloth produces clothing.
Hammering metal produces tools.
Cooking makes food safe and easier to digest.

members.title: Useful and Harmful Changes (Part 2 of 3)
members.content:
Decaying leaves in a compost pit become fertilizer for a school garden.
Other changes are harmful, especially to the environment.
Rust weakens roofing sheets and bridges.
Spoiled food causes illness.

members.title: Useful and Harmful Changes (Part 3 of 3)
members.content:
Burning plastic and other household waste releases smoke and toxic gases into the air, which is why the practice is discouraged and is covered by the Ecological Solid Waste Management Act.
Learning to tell useful changes from harmful ones is what turns this lesson from a list of observations into a habit of responsible decision-making.
